To resist something means to hold firm against a force that is trying to affect you, change you, overcome you, or pull you somewhere you don't want to go.

Imagine someone pushing a heavy door. You plant your feet and push back from the other side. That act of pushing back — refusing to let the door swing open — is resisting. You are not just standing still; there is a real force on you, and you are working against it.

That image is the soul of the word.
The Two Things Always Present in "Resist"

Every single use of "resist" contains these two elements:

  1. A force — something that pushes, pulls, pressures, tempts, or threatens.
  2. Something that holds firm — a person, a material, or a body that doesn't yield to that force.

You always resist something. That "something" is always some kind of force, whether it's a craving, an army, social pressure, heat, or infection.
The Three Main Ways "Resist" Is Used

1. Resisting urges, temptations, and impulses

This is the most common everyday use. You feel a strong inner pull to do something, but you fight it and don't give in.

  • "She resisted the urge to check her phone during the meeting."
    → The urge was real and strong. She felt it. But she fought it.
  • "He resisted the temptation to shout back."
    → Shouting was appealing in the moment, but he held himself back.
  • "I tried to resist the dessert, but I couldn't."
    → He attempted to hold firm, but the temptation won.

One crucial thing to notice here: "resist" admits that the force is real. It has genuine pull over you. If you say "I don't eat sugar," you're describing a simple habit. But if you say "I resist sugar," you're saying: sugar tempts me, it pulls at me — and I fight that pull. There is a struggle involved. You only resist things that actually have power over you.

2. Resisting outside pressure, opposition, or authority

Here, an external force — a person, a group, a government, an enemy — is trying to make you do something, change your mind, or overcome you. You push back, refuse, or fight.

  • "The soldiers resisted the enemy's attack for three days."
    → They fought back; they didn't let the enemy break through.
  • "The workers resisted the new policy."
    → They actively opposed it; they refused to accept it without a fight.
  • "She resisted the pressure to change her answer."
    → Others pushed her hard to change, but she held firm.
  • "He resisted arrest."
    → He physically fought against being taken by the police.

This kind of resistance is often active — it involves doing something to hold your ground.

3. Resisting physical forces (used for materials and the body)

Objects, materials, and even the human body can "resist" something. This means they are not easily affected or damaged by a particular force or substance. No intention is required here — the material simply has properties that hold firm.

  • "This coating resists rust."
    → The coating doesn't let rust form on it.
  • "The building was designed to resist earthquakes."
    → Its structure can withstand earthquake forces without collapsing.
  • "The immune system resists infection."
    → It fights back against bacteria and viruses.
  • "Some bacteria have learned to resist antibiotics."
    → The antibiotics no longer affect them; they hold firm against the drug.
"Resist" Always Implies a Real, Present Force

This is the single most important thing to understand about this word.

You use "resist" only when a genuine force is at work — something that actually has the power to affect you. The word quietly acknowledges: yes, this force is real, yes it is powerful, and yes, something is holding firm against it anyway.

This is what separates "resist" from simply "not doing" something. Not doing something is passive. Resisting is active — there is something to push back against.

Resistance doesn't guarantee success. You can resist and still be overcome.

  • "She resisted for as long as she could, but eventually gave in."
  • "The country resisted for months before it finally surrendered."
  • "He tried to resist the medication's side effects, but they were too strong."

The struggle is resistance, regardless of whether you ultimately win or lose.

You can also resist to different degrees:

  • "She barely resisted the urge." → She almost gave in; it was a weak resistance.
  • "He successfully resisted." → The resistance worked completely.

One of the most common uses in everyday English is "can't resist" — meaning the force is so powerful that holding firm is impossible.

  • "I can't resist chocolate." → Chocolate tempts me too strongly; I always give in.
  • "She couldn't resist smiling." → The smile came even though she didn't intend it.
  • "The offer was too good to resist." → Nobody could hold firm against such a tempting deal.

When something is irresistible, it means no one could possibly hold firm against it — the force is simply too great.

Resist vs. Avoid
To avoid something means to stay away from it before it reaches you — you steer clear of the problem early. To resist means the thing is already right in front of you, pushing at you, and you hold firm in the middle of that encounter. You avoid dangerous neighborhoods; you resist someone who tries to rob you once you're there.

Resist vs. Refuse
To refuse means to say no to an offer or a demand. It's about rejection. Resist is broader — you can resist things that aren't offers at all, like gravity, an urge, or an invading army.

Resist vs. Withstand
These are very close and often interchangeable. The small difference: withstand leans toward enduring or surviving a force without being destroyed. Resist often carries the sense of actively fighting or pushing back. You withstand a terrible storm (you survive it); you resist someone who is trying to control you (you actively push back). But in many sentences, either word works.
A Final Image to Lock It In

Picture a river current pushing against a large rock. The water presses hard, constantly, from every angle. The rock doesn't move. It doesn't drift away with the current. It holds its ground. That is resistance — a force meeting a counter-force, and the counter-force refusing to yield.

The word "resist" always captures this dynamic: something pushing, something holding. Whether it's a person fighting temptation, soldiers defending a city, or a material holding against corrosion — the word always means the same thing at its heart. A force is present. Something is not giving in.
